questions.explanation: #9 says he is being convinced a bounty program may not be a good idea, prefers hiring full-time bug hunters to reviewers, and suggests discretionary coinholder bonuses with no formal guarantee. The retainer option is valens's proposal in #8, which he was replying to but does not adopt; he does not name which replies persuaded him.
options: That the bond should be replaced by a flat 1 USDC fee like Immunefi's, keeping a formal guaranteed bounty for existential bugs.
That Taylor Hornby was a poor example, so rewarding exceptional reporters should be dropped from the proposal altogether.
That a bounty program may not be a good idea; coinholders could vote a discretionary bonus for a truly existential bug, with no formal guarantee.
That dedicated reviewers on retainer are the right answer, so the money should pay several of them well and keep submissions open.
questions.prompt: In #9, what shift in thowar2's view is stated?

questions.explanation: #7 asks whether they were paid to review bugs full time or were normal engineers with other duties, and compares it to scientists cleaning up spills. It does not deny the overload. The GitHub-advisory point comes from #13, which says engineers lacked a dedicated triager and offers a platform or a triager as the two options.
options: Those reviewers were ordinary engineers fitting bug review around their other duties, not people hired as full-time triagers.
The volume of reports was small, so describing ZF and ZCG as DDOSed overstates what they actually experienced.
The reviewers were overwhelmed because the bounty paid too little, so higher rewards would have attracted fewer spam reports.
The reviewers were overwhelmed because reports arrived through GitHub advisories, which a bounty platform would have avoided.
questions.prompt: In #5, thowar2 said ZF and ZCG already had multiple people reviewing bugs and were effectively DDOSed. How did #7 answer?

questions.explanation: #1 says the cost of submitting should exceed the cost of AI generation plus the expected payout, so rejected reports lose money while confident submitters take the risk, and forfeited bonds can fund human and AI reviewers. #5 adds that it opens the doors to real reviewers. The 'keep out independent researchers' option is the critics' reading (#2, #8), not what supporters intended.
options: To keep out independent researchers so that only established auditors submit, which lowers the review load.
To make a rejected submission a real financial loss so slop is not worth sending, while reporters confident in their finding accept the risk.
To replace human reviewers with an automated check, with submitters' payments covering the cost of the AI that runs it.
To charge every researcher a fixed entry fee whatever the outcome, so the program pays for itself and rewards stay high.
questions.prompt: How did supporters of the bond describe what it is for?

questions.explanation: #5 argues AI has changed the economics so reporting costs almost nothing while review is expensive, which leaves reports unreviewed without a cost. #17 says to assume bad actors 99+% of the time but does not present a fee as a way to find honest ones, #13 only describes platform fees, and #29 proposes a fee to self-fund while keeping non-critical rewards low.
options: Because 99+% of submitters are bad actors, a fee is the only way to pick out the rare honest one, who can then be paid.
Because platforms like Immunefi already charge 1 USDC, Zcash would simply be following the practice of most major projects.
Because a fee funds the whole program, rewards for non-critical bugs can be raised without using any grant money.
Because AI makes reporting nearly free while review stays costly, an unbound program leaves reports unreviewed; a cost opens the doors to real reviewers.
questions.prompt: Which is the best case actually made for charging submitters a cost?

questions.explanation: #8 argues a large bond creates a real barrier that could deter legitimate independent researchers, and #2 adds that the average finder would not bother if they had to pay. The coinholder-vote point is from #6 and concerns rules on Retroactive Grants, not fees. #17 argued the 1 USDC fee was too low, which is a case for a higher cost, not against one.
options: Coinholder votes cannot legitimately be restricted, so a fee would be overridden whenever coinholders choose to pay a bounty.
A fee would not deter AI-generated spam, because spammers can cheaply pay it, so only a ban on AI-written submissions could work.
A cost to submit is a barrier for independent researchers who are not well-funded, while disclosure should be as frictionless as possible for credible findings.
A fee would let the Foundation profit from rejected reports, giving it a reason to reject legitimate findings.
questions.prompt: Which is the best case actually made against requiring a bond or entry fee?

questions.explanation: #25, replying to #21, says flooding is an asymmetric economic attack. #26 replies it is not one, since nobody is paid before maintainers endorse a bug, and says to hire a triager; thowar2 does not reply and nobody concedes. #30 gives an example of low volume under a fee but does not claim to settle the point.
options: Contested: #25 says no system survives it unless the economics change, #26 says nothing is drained because nobody is paid before maintainers endorse a bug, and neither gives way.
Conceded: thowar2 accepted in #25 that nobody is paid before a bug is endorsed, so the attack framing no longer applies.
Settled for the bond: #30's Solana example showed that programs without a fee are overwhelmed, which #26 accepted.
Unanswered: nobody replied to #25 after it was posted, and no one disputes that no system can survive such an attack.
questions.prompt: Where does the dispute over whether mass submission of fake reports is an 'asymmetric economic attack' stand at the end of the thread?

questions.explanation: #30 cites Solana's timed Alpenglow bounty: no third-party platform, a burned 0.5 SOL fee, SOL rewards up to 50K SOL, only about 300 submissions, and advice that a designated person handle triage. The Sherlock example is from #2 and the HackerOne point is from #26.
options: A Solana timed bounty run through a third-party platform such as Immunefi, where a 1 USDC fee deterred slop and every engineer shared the triage.
Solana's Alpenglow bounty on its own site, with a burned 0.5 SOL fee per submission and rewards up to 50K SOL, which drew only about 300 submissions.
Aave's Sherlock program with a $100 USDC entry fee, where bugs were missed and a later hack drained over $100 million in liquidity.
HackerOne, which employs full-time triagers and pays nothing until maintainers endorse a report as a real bug.
questions.prompt: What example did #30 offer in discussing how to run a bounty?

questions.explanation: #14 says platform terms are often incompatible with paying in shielded ZEC, can be exclusionary, and may lead to legal battles and law-enforcement requests; #22 also rules platforms out. The fee option misreads #17, which found the 1 USDC fee too low to deter bad actors. #13 had described platforms as providing spam filtering and AI triage.
options: Platforms charge fees that are too high, which would deter researchers who cannot afford to pay and who are the ones Zcash needs.
Platforms cannot filter AI-generated reports, so the same spam would reach the engineers anyway, only with a middleman added.
Platforms triage too slowly, which would leave critical reports unreviewed for long periods while attackers keep looking.
Their terms of service often conflict with Zcash's philosophy of shielded ZEC payouts, are exclusionary, and could bring legal battles and law-enforcement requests.
questions.prompt: What objection did #14 raise to using a bounty platform such as Immunefi, as floated in #13?
